summary: A dense engine-building game where you design a zoo, playing cards to build enclosures, acquire animals, and trigger conservation projects while juggling appeal, reputation, and a tight action-economy where card slots determine how powerful each action is. It plays slow and cerebral, rewarding a long-view engine that only starts paying off in the back half of the game.
praised: deep, satisfying engine-building with a strong theme
gorgeous animal art and production value
high replayability from varied player powers and card pool
criticised: long playtime and heavy analysis paralysis, especially with new players
steep learning curve and rulebook complexity
slow start can feel unrewarding until the engine kicks in
conservation/appeal icon soup takes a while to parse

interaction.kind: drafting from a shared card display and racing for endgame bonus tiles
interaction.detail: Each player builds their own zoo on their own board, and interaction is largely limited to occasionally taking a card or icon slot before someone else wants it, or racing to claim a conservation/association bonus first. The vast majority of decisions and scoring happen entirely within a player's own tableau, independent of what rivals are doing.
interaction.said: Frequently described as "multiplayer solitaire" or "parallel optimization" despite its acclaim — the common complaint is that you barely need to watch what opponents do

sources: Appeal gained from animals housed in your zoo
Appeal from sponsor and bonus cards
Conservation points from supporting conservation projects
Conservation points from university/partner-zoo action cards
end-of-game bonus icons (hourglass) on played cards
scoring.how_you_win: Build up Appeal by collecting and housing animals, and build up Conservation by supporting conservation projects; when the two markers meet on the shared scoring track, one final round is played and whoever has the highest combined Appeal-plus-Conservation total wins.
